1. The animation shows a grid of historical starting months. Each cell is one possible month to buy a home, and the cell's color says whether a buyer or a renter came out ahead. Light cells mean the buyer was ahead after ten years. Dark cells mean the renter was ahead. The data sources are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. The labels say "ILLUSTRATIVE", "US only" and "history, not a forecast".

2. The grid is mostly light, so buyers were ahead in most months. A band of dark cells runs down the middle, and it shifts from frame to frame. In frames 1 and 2 the dark band is in the center, with one light gap inside it. In frames 3 to 6 a dark strip grows along the left edge, and the central band moves and changes shape. In frames 5 and 6 a caption appears: "held five years: buyer ahead in 74.4%". The date label stays at "January 1991" throughout.

3. In this historical data, buying beat renting in most starting months, but not in all of them. The caption says that when the home was held for five years, the buyer came out ahead in about 74% of cases. That leaves about a quarter of cases where renting was cheaper. The dark clusters show that the outcome depends on when you bought. Some periods favored renters, probably when prices or rates were unfavorable.

4. The animation gives no direct advice. A viewer could take away that buying has usually paid off over long holding periods, but that the result isn't guaranteed and depends on timing.

5. The advice in 4 is my own conclusion. The on-screen text only reports the historical share, 74.4%, and warns that this is "history, not a forecast". It never tells the viewer to buy or to rent. I'm also not sure how the five-year caption relates to the ten-year legend, because the image doesn't explain it.
